pedagogy.summary: Simplifying is the equivalence principle run in reverse: instead of multiplying numerator and denominator by n, you DIVIDE both by a common factor, which regroups the same quantity into fewer, larger pieces without changing its value. Simplest form is reached when numerator and denominator share no common factor but 1 (i.e. you have divided by the HCF). The same machinery — finding a common multiple — lets you rewrite two fractions over a shared denominator. Both skills rest on one idea from Year 5: a/b = (n×a)/(n×b), so a/b = (a÷n)/(b÷n). Teach simplification as 'un-grouping' back to the coarsest partition, not as a memorised rule.
bestPractices: Anchor the procedure to the equivalence principle already learned: show that dividing top and bottom by the same number is the inverse of multiplying by the same number, so the value is unchanged — use a fraction wall or area model where 6/8 and 3/4 occupy identical length.

Connect directly to common factors/multiples work: to simplify, divide by a common factor (fastest via the HCF); to find a common denominator, use a common multiple (efficiently the LCM). Make the number theory visible, not incidental.

Distinguish 'an equivalent, simpler fraction' from 'simplest form' explicitly — a child who writes 6/8 = 3/4 has simplified; a child who writes 6/8 = ... but stops at a form still sharing a factor has not finished. Ask 'can you go further?' every time.
Use dividing-by-HCF as the efficient route but accept repeated division by any common factor (÷2 then ÷2) as valid — the concept, not the shortcut, is the target.
Contrast simplifying with the illegal move of adding or subtracting the same number from top and bottom, which does change the value; have children test 6/8 vs (6-2)/(8-2)=4/6 against the wall.
keyRepresentations: Fraction wall / bar model where equivalent fractions align to identical length (6/8 sits exactly over 3/4)
Area model / grid that can be re-partitioned by merging small cells into larger groups (24 cells shaded 18, re-grouped into 4 columns of which 3 are shaded → 3/4)
Factor pairs and HCF listing beside the fraction (18 = 2×3×3, 24 = 2×2×2×3, common = 2×3 = 6)
Number line showing 18/24 and 3/4 landing on the identical point
Common-multiple ladder for the common-denominator task (thirds and eighths both re-cut into 24ths)
commonMisconceptions: Simplifying by SUBTRACTING a common amount from numerator and denominator (6/8 → 4/6 by taking 2 from each) instead of dividing — treats the fraction additively.
Stopping before simplest form: dividing 18/24 by 2 to get 9/12 and calling it done, not checking for a remaining common factor.
Operating on only one part — dividing the numerator but not the denominator (or renaming only the denominator when finding a common denominator).
Believing simplifying changes the fraction's value ('3/4 is bigger than 6/8 because 4 is fewer pieces') rather than renaming the same quantity.
When finding a common denominator, changing the denominators to match but forgetting to scale the numerators correspondingly.

learn.summary: Teach simplifying as the equivalence principle run in reverse: dividing numerator and denominator by a common factor regroups the same quantity into fewer, larger pieces without changing its value, just as multiplying both by n does. Simplest form is reached when numerator and denominator share no common factor but 1 (you have divided by the HCF). The same number-theory machinery — finding a common multiple — lets two fractions be rewritten over a shared denominator. Anchor to the Year 5 fact a/b = (n×a)/(n×b), so a/b = (a÷n)/(b÷n), and treat simplification as 'un-grouping' back to the coarsest partition, not a memorised rule.

activities.title: Un-grouping a bar: 18/24 back to simplest form
feedback: If the bar length stays fixed while the label changes, the value is unchanged — that non-movement IS the point: same quantity, fewer pieces.
If a chosen divisor leaves leftover cells that won't tile evenly, it is not a common factor of both numbers — that felt 'doesn't fit' is what 'common factor' means.
If you stop at 9/12, ask 'can you go further? do 9 and 12 still share a factor?' — 9/12 is correct but not finished.
Dividing by the HCF (6) reaches simplest form in one step; for 18/24, ÷2 then ÷3 is equally valid and reaches the same place — the concept, not the shortcut, is the target.
activities.rationale: A re-partitionable area/bar model lets the learner perform the regrouping and see the fixed length, making 'same value, fewer pieces' and 'common factor' felt rather than merely told. An optional divisor-snap mechanism (groups form only when the divisor divides both numbers, otherwise leftovers appear) may make the failure of a non-common factor concrete; a 'simplest form' indicator that stays dark until no factor above 1 remains may discourage stopping early. These interaction examples are illustrative proposals, not required and not empirically validated.
sourceClaims: Understanding equivalent fractions — that a fraction can be renamed by multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same number without changing its value — is foundational, and instruction should build simplifying on this principle using visual number-line and area models rather than rote rules.
Pupils should use common factors to simplify fractions and use common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination (Year 6 statutory content).
learnerActions: Start with a bar partitioned into 24 cells with 18 shaded, labelled 18/24.
Choose a number to 'group by' (a divisor) and merge the cells into equal groups of that size, watching the fraction label recompute (e.g. grouping in sixes gives 4 fat groups with 3 shaded → 3/4).

Observe that for each valid grouping of the original 24-cell bar the shaded LENGTH does not move while the label takes an equivalent form (grouping by 2 → 9/12, by 3 → 6/8, by 6 → 3/4) — the quantity is unchanged, only the cut is coarser.
Deliberately try a divisor that is NOT a common factor (e.g. 5): notice the cells will not group evenly and leftovers remain, so that divisor is rejected.
Keep going until no grouping beyond 1 is possible, then state the simplest form and name the HCF (6) that would have reached it in one step.
Also try the valid repeated route (÷2 then ÷3) and confirm it lands on the same 3/4.
activities.intendedInsight: Dividing both parts by a common factor regroups the same quantity into fewer, larger equal pieces, leaving the value (length) unchanged; simplest form is reached only when no common factor above 1 remains.

activities.title: Common denominator by re-cutting to a shared multiple
feedback: If you changed only the denominators (2/24, 5/24) the fractions now mean far less than before — re-cutting the whole into more parts means you must count correspondingly more shaded parts.
Both 24 and 48 are common multiples of 3 and 8, so both give a valid shared denominator; 24 is the smallest (the LCM).
Match the scaling factor: 3→24 is ×8, so 2→16; 8→24 is ×3, so 5→15.
activities.rationale: Re-cutting two bars to a shared grid makes a common multiple visible as a partition both fractions can sit on, and re-shading exposes the classic error of changing denominators without scaling numerators. A ladder of common multiples may make the LCM choice explicit. These are proposed scaffolds, not validated interventions.
sourceClaims: Pupils should use common factors to simplify fractions and use common multiples to express fractions in the same denomination (Year 6 statutory content).
learnerActions: Place bars for 2/3 and 5/8 (or thirds and eighths) side by side.
Find a common multiple of 3 and 8 to use as the shared denominator (24 works; 48 also works — find the smallest, the LCM).
Re-cut BOTH bars into 24ths and rewrite each fraction: 2/3 = 16/24 and 5/8 = 15/24, scaling each numerator by the same factor used on its denominator.
Check: 2/3 becomes 16/24 because both parts were multiplied by 8; 5/8 becomes 15/24 because both were multiplied by 3 — the numerator must scale with the denominator.
Compare using 24 versus 48 and explain why 24 is the smallest denominator that works.
activities.intendedInsight: Expressing fractions over a common denominator uses a common multiple (efficiently the LCM); when you change a denominator you must scale its numerator by the same factor, or you change the quantity.

activities.title: Divide versus subtract: testing the illegal move
feedback: If 4/6 and 6/8 land at different lengths on the wall, the value changed — subtracting from both parts is not simplifying.
If 3/4 and 6/8 land at the same length, dividing both parts preserved the value — that is the legal move.
activities.rationale: Directly testing the additive misconception against a length model lets the learner see the value shift, addressing the common belief that any identical change to both parts is harmless. The wall comparison is the diagnostic surface.
sourceClaims: Understanding equivalent fractions — that a fraction can be renamed by multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same number without changing its value — is foundational, and instruction should build simplifying on this principle using visual number-line and area models rather than rote rules.
learnerActions: Take 6/8 and perform the illegal move of subtracting the same amount from both parts: (6−2)/(8−2) = 4/6.
Lay 6/8 and 4/6 on the same fraction wall or bar and compare their lengths.
Observe that the lengths differ, so subtracting the same number from top and bottom DID change the value.
Contrast with dividing both parts by 2: 6/8 → 3/4, whose length matches 6/8 exactly.
State what the test showed: multiplying or dividing both parts by the same non-zero number keeps the value, but subtracting the same amount from both parts generally changes it (as 6/8 → 4/6 did).
activities.intendedInsight: Simplifying is division of both parts by a common factor, not subtraction of a common amount; the additive move generally changes the value (it keeps it only in special cases such as fractions equal to 1), so it is not a valid equivalence method.

activities.title: Check and explain (assessment of output)
feedback: Only 3/4 among 9/12, 6/8, 3/4, 12/16 is fully simplified; the others still share a factor with their denominator.
9/12 is not wrong, just not finished — 9 and 12 still share a factor of 3, so simplify again to 3/4.

For 18/24, answers like 16/22 or 12/18 (from subtracting a common amount from both parts) or 3/24 (dividing only the numerator) reveal the wrong operation, not just a stopping error — revisit the bar model.
activities.rationale: Short checkable items with distractors built from the subtract-instead-of-divide and stop-early errors make this a diagnostic assessment of the output. Recognition and short-answer items check the result; by themselves they do not elicit the regrouping insight, so this complements rather than replaces the manipulative work.
learnerActions: Write 18/24 in its simplest form and show the working (via HCF 6, or ÷2 then ÷3).
Rewrite 2/3 and 5/8 so they share the same denominator.
Identify which of 9/12, 6/8, 3/4, 12/16 is fully simplified and explain why the others are not.
Explain why dividing both parts by the same non-zero number does not change the value, while subtracting the same amount from both parts generally does.
Answer: your friend simplified 18/24 to 9/12 and stopped — is 9/12 wrong, or just not finished? How do you know?
activities.intendedInsight: Simplest form and common-denominator rewriting can be stated and justified, distinguishing a correct-but-unfinished answer from a wrong operation.

constraints: Build simplifying on the equivalence principle learners met in Year 5 (a/b = (n×a)/(n×b)); do not teach it as an isolated rule.
Make the number theory explicit: divide by a common factor (efficiently the HCF) to simplify; use a common multiple (efficiently the LCM) for a common denominator.
Always ask 'can you go further?' — distinguish 'an equivalent simpler fraction' from 'simplest form'. Stopping at 9/12 is unfinished, not wrong.
Accept repeated division by any common factor (e.g. ÷2 then ÷2 where both divide evenly, or ÷2 then ÷3 for 18/24) as valid; the concept, not the HCF shortcut, is the target.
Simplifying compares and regroups the SAME fraction; no denominator rule 'flips' — dividing both parts by a shared factor is a single consistent operation.

A static tap-to-reveal worked example (e.g. tap to show factor pairs of 18 and 24, highlight the HCF, reveal ÷6 on both parts) can serve as a reference card but does not let the learner try divisors or feel the regrouping; use it alongside, not instead of, hands-on work.
Recognition/short-answer items assess the output (simplest form, common denominator) but do not by themselves elicit the regrouping insight; pair them with construction on a model.
Scale BOTH parts by the same factor: dividing only the numerator, or changing denominators without scaling numerators, changes the quantity.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
One listed source (DfE National Curriculum, Year 6 Fractions) is marked verified:false in the source row; treat its claim as unconfirmed.

Arithmetic self-audit: 18/24 ÷ 6 = 3/4 (correct); HCF(18,24)=6 via 18=2×3×3, 24=2×2×2×3, common 2×3=6 (correct). For a shared denominator of 24, 2/3 = 16/24 (×8) and 5/8 = 15/24 (×3) are correct equivalent rewrites, not a sum. 6/8 with the subtract move gives (6−2)/(8−2)=4/6 (a correct depiction of the misconception).

Clarification on the source assessment's additive-misconception examples: subtracting a common amount from 18/24 can correctly yield 12/18 (subtract 6 from each) or 16/22 (subtract 2 from each) — both are legitimate depictions of the subtract-instead-of-divide error, differing only in the amount removed. The source is NOT internally inconsistent here; the divide-vs-subtract activity simply uses the single, cleaner 6/8 → 4/6 example to keep one consistent base fraction.

The source's catalog fit ratings assert that 3D and in-role dialogue add no conceptual value here. These are medium-fit opinions, not established facts; a conversation could still coach and a spatial model could still illustrate. Guidance retains only the narrow observable point (execution and felt regrouping are what the manipulative directly supports) without asserting that other media are impossible.

The 'the concept lives only in the manipulation' and 'a quiz only assesses' framings from the source are softened to narrow affordances: the checking activity is a complementary assessment of output, and recognition alone does not elicit production of the regrouping.

probeDeeper: You wrote 18/24 = 3/4. How do you know 3/4 is as simple as it gets — could you simplify it further? Why not?
Why does dividing the top and bottom by the same number NOT change the fraction's value, when subtracting the same number from both DOES change it?
Your friend simplified 18/24 to 9/12 and stopped. Is 9/12 wrong, or just not finished? How would you know?
To add 2/3 and 5/8 you first put them over 24. Why 24 — would 48 also work? What is the smallest denominator that works, and how did you find it?
assess.correctAnswer: 18/24 = 3/4 (divide both by the HCF 6, or ÷2 then ÷3). Common denominator 24: 2/3 = 16/24 and 5/8 = 15/24.

errorPatterns.pattern: Simplifies by subtracting the same amount from top and bottom ('take 6 off each: 18/24 becomes 12/18') instead of dividing — treats the fraction additively.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put 18/24 and their subtracted answer on the same bar/wall — the lengths differ, so the value changed. Re-establish that only ×n/n or ÷n/n leaves the quantity unchanged; reteach the equivalence principle.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answer like 12/18 or 4/6 for 6/8; when asked to show working, the child subtracts rather than divides.

errorPatterns.pattern: Stops before simplest form ('18/24 = 9/12, done') — divides by a common factor once but does not check whether the result still shares a factor.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do not reteach — the operation is sound. Prompt 'can you go further? do 9 and 12 still share a factor?' Build the habit of checking for remaining common factors; suggest dividing by the HCF in one step.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Produces a correct-but-not-final equivalent (9/12 or 6/8) and treats the task as complete.

errorPatterns.pattern: Operates on only one part — divides the numerator but leaves the denominator (or, in the common-denominator task, changes denominators to 24 but leaves the numerators unchanged: 2/24 and 5/24).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to the bar: changing the number of parts you count without re-cutting the whole (or vice versa) makes a different quantity. Reteach that equivalence scales BOTH parts by the same factor.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Answers such as 3/24 for simplifying, or 2/24 and 5/24 for the common-denominator half.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot reach an equivalent simpler fraction, or subtracts from both parts; changes denominators without scaling numerators. Does not connect the action to keeping the value the same.
responseLevels.full: Simplifies to 3/4 by dividing both parts by a common factor (ideally the HCF), verifies no common factor remains, and explains that dividing both parts by the same number regroups the same quantity so the value is unchanged. Rewrites 2/3 and 5/8 as 16/24 and 15/24, scaling numerators with denominators, and can justify the choice of 24 as a common multiple. Transfers the reasoning to a new fraction on request.
responseLevels.partial: Divides both parts correctly to produce an equivalent fraction and can find a common denominator, but stops before simplest form, or can execute the steps without explaining why the value is unchanged — lists the procedure without the relational reason.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is 18/24. Write it in its simplest form, and show how you got there. Then rewrite 2/3 and 5/8 so they share the same denominator.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the child work separates the child who DIVIDES both parts (correct) from the child who subtracts a common amount, who divides only one part, or who stops before simplest form. A child reasoning correctly divides top and bottom by a shared factor and checks nothing divides further; a child with the additive misconception produces 16/22 or 4/6-type answers that look plausible but reveal the wrong operation. The common-denominator half exposes whether they scale numerators when they change denominators — the classic partial-credit trap.
